newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU panel makes little progress on EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU panel makes little progress on EMU budget pact.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee ended a scheduled meeting on Tuesday, making little progress on the remaining details of a budget stability pact for countries joining a single currency, monetary sources said.

The committee, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, edged towards a European Commission plan for sanctions on countries which run excessive deficits inside a monetary union, sources added.
But it was still unclear whether the group would fully endorse certain aspects of the plan which penalises countries with annual deficits above three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"There is still some unclarity with respect to the initial fine," said one source familiar with the committee's discussions.

The Commission, the EU's executive, has advocated fining a country 0.2 or 0.3 percent of total output should it exceed the three percent threshold. For each additional percentage point above the limit, another 0.1 percent of GDP would be added to the initial penalty, with a maximum ceiling of 0.5 percent.
While this so-called "linear approach" is largely agreed, the initial penalty is still in dispute, as is the notion of an overall ceiling.
"On these two issues there still seems to be some disagreement," added another official.
A further area of contention is an exact definition of what constitutes an exceptional or temporary economic situation, one that would let a country with an excessive deficit off the hook.
Germany initially proposed that such a situation could be defined as a two percent decline in real GDP over four consecutive quarters.
The Commission, seeking a compromise, has advanced the idea of simply four consecutive quarters of negative growth, leaving the precise degree of economic contraction unspecified.
The committee also focused on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) that links the single currency, the euro, to currencies outside monetary union.

But sources said there was little progress beyond what the European Monetary Institute, Europe's nascent central bank, has already proposed -- a system with the single currency as the anchor and non-participating currencies trading against it in relatively wide bands.

Meanwhile, there was broad agreement that several legal issues regarding the single currency should be clarified as quickly as possible, particularly those relating to the continuity of financial contracts after the start of monetary union, expected in 1999.
